This message is wrong on two counts: (1) SQL expressions ARE implemented — they are deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264, RCE/LFI via DuckDB), so telling users the feature is 'not implemented' misinforms them about why their query fails and what to expect; (2) it exposes the internal camelCase feature-flag name `sqlExpressions` to end users. These stubs exist to replace the DuckDB-backed implementation that was removed for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). However, 'not implemented' is misleading: the functionality was deliberately removed/disabled for security, not merely left unimplemented. Any code path that reaches these methods (e.g. `NewSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` line 30 calls `sql.TablesList`, which will now always fail with 'not implemented') will surface a confusing error. In `NewSQLCommand`, this error is caught and converted to a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest, which hides the real reason. The stubs should return an error that clearly states SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons, so that any path that bypasses the reader-level guard produces an understandable, non-misleading failure rather than a generic 'not implemented'."

      "file": "pkg/expr/sql_command.go",

Consequently `NewSQLCommand` will always fail with `errutil.BadRequest(\"sql-invalid-sql\", ... \"error reading SQL command\")`. The reader-level guard in `pkg/expr/reader.go` blocks the `QueryTypeSQL` path, but `UnmarshalSQLCommand` is a separate entry point (used by the legacy/transform path) that is NOT guarded by `enableSqlExpressions` — it calls `NewSQLCommand` directly. This means: (1) any caller of `UnmarshalSQLCommand` gets a confusing 'error reading SQL command' for every SQL query, with no indication that SQL expressions are disabled; (2) the table-extraction logic is now dead/broken code that always errors. The legacy path should either be guarded with the same disabled check (returning a clear 'SQL expressions are disabled' error) or removed, rather than left calling into a stub that always fails with an opaque message."

This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this PR), but it is in a file central to this change and means empty SQL query results are returned as an empty `TableData` frame rather than `NoData`, which may affect downstream handling of empty results. More importantly, after this PR the function is backed by a stub `DB` whose `RunCommands` always returns an error, so this code path is now unreachable in production — it is dead code that still contains the unsafe string-interpolation pattern. If this code is retained for future re-enablement, the escaping must be fixed (e.g. via proper parameterized queries or a robust escaping function); as it stands, leaving unsafe SQL string construction in the tree is a hazard if the stub is ever replaced with a real implementation. While Go tooling ignores trailing comments on require lines, this is clearly a corruption (likely from an automated tool that appends `// indirect` and collided with an existing comment) and should be cleaned up to just `// indirect` (or the correct annotation). findings.title: enableSqlExpressions is dead code that always returns false, making the feature-flag check meaningless
findings.body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches. This means the feature flag `sqlExpressions` is never actually consulted: SQL expressions are unconditionally disabled regardless of whether the flag is enabled. The intent (per the PR description, which says the flag 'still exists in the codebase') appears to be to keep the flag as an escape hatch, but as written the flag has no effect. If the flag is meant to re-enable SQL expressions for users who explicitly opt in, the function should return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (or the inverse logic corrected); if SQL expressions are meant to be permanently disabled, the flag check and the misleading function should be removed entirely rather than left as dead code that gives the false impression the flag still controls behavior.

findings.title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading and leaks internal naming
findings.body: When SQL expressions are rejected, the code returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is wrong on two counts: (1) SQL expressions ARE implemented — they are deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264, RCE/LFI via DuckDB), so telling users the feature is 'not implemented' misinforms them about why their query fails and what to expect; (2) it exposes the internal camelCase feature-flag name `sqlExpressions` to end users. The message should clearly state that SQL expressions are disabled, e.g. 'SQL expressions are disabled' or reference the security advisory, so users understand this is a deliberate security restriction rather than a missing feature.

These stubs exist to replace the DuckDB-backed implementation that was removed for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). However, 'not implemented' is misleading: the functionality was deliberately removed/disabled for security, not merely left unimplemented. Any code path that reaches these methods (e.g. `NewSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` line 30 calls `sql.TablesList`, which will now always fail with 'not implemented') will surface a confusing error. In `NewSQLCommand`, this error is caught and converted to a generic 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest, which hides the real reason. The stubs should return an error that clearly states SQL expressions are disabled for security reasons, so that any path that bypasses the reader-level guard produces an understandable, non-misleading failure rather than a generic 'not implemented'.

findings.title: NewSQLCommand can still be reached and now always fails with a misleading error after DuckDB removal
findings.body: `NewSQLCommand` (and `UnmarshalSQLCommand`, which calls it) still calls `sql.TablesList(rawSQL)` at line 30 to extract table names from the SQL. After this PR, `sql.TablesList` is backed by the stub `DB` whose `RunCommands` returns `errors.New("not implemented")`, so `TablesList` will always return an error. Consequently `NewSQLCommand` will always fail with `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", ... "error reading SQL command")`. The reader-level guard in `pkg/expr/reader.go` blocks the `QueryTypeSQL` path, but `UnmarshalSQLCommand` is a separate entry point (used by the legacy/transform path) that is NOT guarded by `enableSqlExpressions` — it calls `NewSQLCommand` directly. This means: (1) any caller of `UnmarshalSQLCommand` gets a confusing 'error reading SQL command' for every SQL query, with no indication that SQL expressions are disabled; (2) the table-extraction logic is now dead/broken code that always errors. The legacy path should either be guarded with the same disabled check (returning a clear 'SQL expressions are disabled' error) or removed, rather than left calling into a stub that always fails with an opaque message.

findings.title: Dead code: rsp.Values is unconditionally overwritten after the NoData branch
findings.body: In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.NoData{Frame: frame}}` (lines 110-114), but then immediately and unconditionally overwrites it at lines 116-118 with `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}}`. The `NoData` assignment is therefore dead code and has no effect. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this PR), but it is in a file central to this change and means empty SQL query results are returned as an empty `TableData` frame rather than `NoData`, which may affect downstream handling of empty results. It should be fixed by adding a `return` or `else` so the `NoData` branch is actually reachable, or by removing the dead branch.

findings.title: SQL string escaping via single-quote doubling is insufficient and the code path is now unreachable dead code
findings.body: `TablesList` builds a DuckDB command with `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This is a fragile, incomplete escaping approach for embedding arbitrary SQL inside a SQL string literal (it does not handle backslashes or other escape sequences that DuckDB's parser may interpret). More importantly, after this PR the function is backed by a stub `DB` whose `RunCommands` always returns an error, so this code path is now unreachable in production — it is dead code that still contains the unsafe string-interpolation pattern. If this code is retained for future re-enablement, the escaping must be fixed (e.g. via proper parameterized queries or a robust escaping function); as it stands, leaving unsafe SQL string construction in the tree is a hazard if the stub is ever replaced with a real implementation. Ideally this function should be removed along with the DuckDB dependency, or clearly marked as disabled.

The trailing comment is malformed — it appears to be a merge/rebase artifact where `// indirect` was concatenated with a version string `indirect0.0.0-20240809095826-8eb5495c0b2a`, producing nonsense text. It indicates the go.mod was not properly regenerated/verified after the dependency removal.

findings.title: No test coverage for the SQL-expression disabled guard or the stub DB behavior
findings.body: This PR adds a security-critical guard (`enableSqlExpressions` returning false, causing `QueryTypeSQL` to be rejected) and replaces the DuckDB-backed `DB` with a stub that always errors. Neither change appears to be accompanied by tests: there is no test asserting that a `QueryTypeSQL` query is rejected with the disabled error, no test asserting that `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` fail gracefully (or are blocked) now that `sql.TablesList` always errors, and no test for the new stub `DB` methods. Given this is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI), a regression test that verifies SQL expressions cannot be executed through both the `ReadQuery` path and the `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path is important to prevent the vulnerability from being reintroduced if the guard is accidentally removed or bypassed.
